n: The Bible opens not with a battle between gods, as Babylonian myths did, but with one God speaking a world into order. 'Without form and void' (Latin inanis et vacua) describes chaos being tamed, not matter being fought. The 'Spirit of God moved over the waters' is read by Christians as the first glimpse of the Trinity at work.

Light is created on the first day, the sun and moon only on the fourth. Readers ancient and modern have noticed. The text is arranged as a week of work — three days of separating (light, waters, land), three of filling (lights, fish and birds, animals and humans) — a liturgical poem, not a laboratory report.

t: 'Let us make man to our image'
n: The plural 'let us' puzzled readers for centuries: Jewish tradition heard God addressing his heavenly court, Christian readers heard the Trinity. 'Image and likeness' is the ground of human dignity in both faiths — every person, not only kings, bears the royal stamp of God.

God does not tire; the rest of the seventh day is a model. It founds the Sabbath, the first thing in Scripture called 'holy'. Christians later moved their weekly rest to Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, calling it 'the eighth day' — creation begun again.

'Knowledge of good and evil' means deciding for oneself what is good and evil — moral autonomy, not information. Every other tree is given freely; the single prohibition makes obedience possible and love real. Jerome's Latin morte morieris, 'thou shalt die the death', is a Hebrew intensifier: 'you will surely die'.

Christians call this verse the first promise of a redeemer: the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. The Vulgate famously reads ipsa conteret, 'she shall crush', which shaped centuries of Marian art (the Virgin standing on a serpent). The Hebrew has 'he' — the offspring himself. Both readings point the same direction: victory over evil through a child of Eve.

Before expelling them, God himself makes clothes for the couple — judgment wrapped in care. The cherubim and flaming sword guard the way back to the tree of life; the Book of Revelation ends with that way reopened (Rev 22:14). The whole Bible is the story of the road back to Eden.

Cain's sneer is the first recorded lie to God's face. The answer of the whole Torah is yes. 'The voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me' introduces a theme that runs to the Letter to the Hebrews, where Christ's blood 'speaketh better than that of Abel' (Heb 12:24) — pleading mercy instead of vengeance.

t: The 'sons of God' and the giants
n: One of the strangest passages in Scripture. Early readers (and the Book of Enoch) took the 'sons of God' as fallen angels; later Jewish and Christian teachers read them as the godly line of Seth marrying into the line of Cain. The 'giants' (Hebrew Nephilim) belong to a world sliding into violence before the Flood.

Three hundred cubits long (about 135 metres), with three decks and a single door — a floating box, not a ship, with no rudder: God steers. Mesopotamia had older flood stories (Gilgamesh, Atrahasis); Genesis retells the theme with one just God instead of quarrelling ones. 1 Peter 3:20 makes the ark a picture of baptism.

t: Sacrifice and the promise of seasons
n: Noah's first act on dry land is worship. God's response — 'I will no more curse the earth... seedtime and harvest, cold and heat... shall not cease' — is the charter of a stable, trustworthy creation. The rainbow of the next chapter is a war-bow hung up in the sky, pointed away from the earth.

t: Noe's drunkenness and the curse of Chanaan
n: The first vineyard, the first drunkenness. Noe curses not Cham, who saw him naked, but Cham's son Chanaan — a text written to explain Israel's later dominance over the Canaanites. Its abuse to justify the enslavement of Africans is one of the darkest chapters in the history of biblical interpretation.

The tower is a ziggurat, a Mesopotamian temple-mountain; its builders want to 'make a name' for themselves. God's scattering is both judgment and mercy — limiting how far a united arrogance can go. Pentecost (Acts 2), where people of every tongue hear one message, is Babel reversed.

Three promises — land, descendants, and blessing for 'all the kindred of the earth' — govern everything that follows in the Bible. Abram is seventy-five, childless, and told to walk away from everything. Paul makes this the model of faith: he believed a promise he could not see (Rom 4).

A king of Salem (Jerusalem) appears from nowhere, brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and vanishes. Psalm 109 (110) and the Letter to the Hebrews make him a type of Christ — a priest not by descent but by God's word. The Roman Canon of the Mass still names 'thy high priest Melchisedech'.

Abram simply trusts, and God counts it as righteousness. This single verse became the hinge of the Reformation debate on faith and works. Paul cites it (Rom 4, Gal 3) to say the promise came before the Law; James cites it (Jas 2) to say faith proved itself in what Abraham did.

Ancient covenants were sealed by cutting animals in two and passing between the halves — 'may this be done to me if I break my word'. Here only God, as a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire, passes through. The covenant rests on God's oath alone; Abram is asleep.

Abraham sees three men and addresses them as one 'Lord'. Christian tradition saw here a foreshadowing of the Trinity — the subject of Rublev's famous icon. Hospitality to strangers becomes a sacred duty: 'some have entertained angels unawares' (Heb 13:2).

'Wilt thou destroy the just with the wicked?' Abraham haggles God down from fifty righteous to ten. The scene establishes that God's justice can be argued with in prayer, and that a few righteous people can shield a whole city — an idea Jesus echoes when he calls his disciples 'the salt of the earth'.

Fire and brimstone on the cities of the plain, and Lot's wife turned to salt for looking back. Jesus' three-word warning, 'Remember Lot's wife' (Luke 17:32), makes her the type of the person who cannot let go. The Dead Sea's salt formations still bear her name for tourists.

The hardest chapter in Genesis. God asks for the son on whom every promise depends; Abraham obeys without a word of complaint; Isaac carries the wood himself. Jews call it the Akedah and read it on the New Year; Christians see the Father who did not spare his own Son (Rom 8:32). 'God will provide' (Dominus videbit) names the mountain — later the site of the Temple.

t: A birthright for a bowl of lentils
n: Esau, famished, trades the rights of the firstborn for red stew. The story is told with contempt for his shrug: 'he ate, and drank, and went his way'. Hebrews 12:16 makes him the type of the person who sells the eternal for the immediate. Jacob's cunning is not praised either; both brothers will pay for this.

'The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.' A blind father, a scheming mother, goat-skins on the arms — and a blessing that, once spoken, cannot be recalled. The Bible does not excuse the deceit; Jacob will be deceived in turn by Laban (chapter 29) and by his own sons (chapter 37).

Alone and running from his brother, Jacob sleeps on a stone and sees a stairway with angels, God standing above it. 'This is no other but the house of God, and the gate of heaven' (Bethel means 'house of God'). Jesus applies the image to himself: the angels ascend and descend 'upon the Son of man' (John 1:51).

'They seemed but a few days, because of the greatness of his love.' Then the trick: in the morning it is Lia (Leah). The deceiver is deceived, and works seven more years. The two sisters and their maids will bear the twelve tribes; Rachel's tomb near Bethlehem is still a pilgrimage site.

On the night before he must face Esau, Jacob wrestles a mysterious man until daybreak, is wounded in the hip, and refuses to let go without a blessing. He receives a new name, Israel, 'he who strives with God'. The nation is named after a limping man who would not let go of God.

The Hebrew describes a long-sleeved tunic — the dress of someone who does not do manual work. Jacob repeats the favouritism that wrecked his own family. The Joseph story (chapters 37–50) is the longest continuous narrative in Genesis and reads like a novel: betrayal, prison, power, and a forgiveness that saves the whole family.

A widow denied the husband owed her by custom dresses as a prostitute and conceives twins by her father-in-law Juda. When he moves to burn her, she produces his seal and staff, and he admits: 'she is juster than I'. Matthew's genealogy names her, unembarrassed, among Jesus' ancestors.

Joseph reveals himself to the brothers who sold him and refuses to see it as their crime alone: 'not by your counsel was I sent hither, but by the will of God'. Genesis 50:20 will put it more sharply — 'you thought evil against me, but God turned it into good'. This is the Bible's first full statement of providence.

t: The lion of Juda and the sceptre
n: Jacob's deathbed blessing gives Judah the kingship: 'the sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda... till he come that is to be sent'. The Vulgate's donec veniat qui mittendus est was read as a prophecy of the Messiah, and Revelation 5:5 calls Christ 'the lion of the tribe of Juda'.

The Hebrew word for the basket is the same as for Noe's ark — a small ark on the Nile. Pharaoh's own daughter rescues the child his decree condemned, and his mother is paid to nurse him. 'Moses' is an Egyptian name (as in Thut-mose); the text hears the Hebrew 'drawn out'.

A bush burning without being consumed: the Fathers saw an image of God's presence that does not destroy what it fills, and of the Virgin who bore God without harm. 'Put off the shoes from thy feet' — the first 'holy ground' in the Bible is not a temple but a place where God speaks.

Asked his name, God answers Ego sum qui sum. The Hebrew YHWH — four consonants Jews do not pronounce, reading 'Adonai' (Lord) instead — is rendered Dominus in the Vulgate and 'the LORD' in most English Bibles. Jesus' 'before Abraham was made, I am' (John 8:58) claims this name.

Blood, frogs, gnats, flies, cattle plague, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, death of the firstborn. Each strikes something Egypt worshipped — the Nile, the sun, Pharaoh's own divine line. Ten times Pharaoh's heart is hardened, sometimes by himself, sometimes by God: the text holds both without resolving it.

A lamb without blemish, its blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste: the Pasch (Passover) becomes Israel's founding memory, kept every spring to this day. John's Gospel times the crucifixion to the slaughter of the lambs and calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God'; Paul says plainly, 'Christ our pasch is sacrificed' (1 Cor 5:7).

The crossing of the Red Sea (Hebrew 'Sea of Reeds') is the central act of salvation in the Old Testament, sung about in Psalms and prophets. Paul calls it a baptism (1 Cor 10:2); the Easter Vigil reads this chapter every year while the newly baptised wait at the font.

The name manna is the question the Israelites asked — man hu, 'what is it?' A daily bread that cannot be hoarded, it teaches trust one day at a time. Jesus sets himself against it: 'your fathers did eat manna and are dead... I am the living bread' (John 6).

At Raphidim the people quarrel and Moses strikes the rock. Paul says startlingly, 'they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). The place is named Massa and Meriba, 'testing' and 'quarrel' — Psalm 94 warns, 'harden not your hearts as at Meriba'.

Hebrew calls them the 'ten words', not commandments. Catholics and Lutherans number them one way (the prohibition of idols folded into the first; two commandments on coveting), Jews, Orthodox and Reformed another. The first tablet concerns God, the second one's neighbour — the two loves Jesus later names as the whole Law.

Moses reads the law, the people say 'we will do it', and he sprinkles them with blood: 'this is the blood of the covenant'. At the Last Supper Jesus uses exactly these words of the cup (Matt 26:28). The covenant at Sinai and the new covenant are meant to be heard together.

A gold-covered chest holding the tablets, with two cherubim on its lid — the 'propitiatory' or mercy seat, where God promises 'I will speak to thee'. It went before Israel into battle, was captured by the Philistines, brought to Jerusalem by David, and vanished when Babylon burned the Temple. Its fate is unknown.

Forty days without Moses and the people build a god they can see. Aaron's excuse — 'I cast the gold into the fire, and there came out this calf' — is one of the Bible's dry jokes. The calf was probably meant as a throne or footstool for the invisible God; the sin was making God manageable.

t: 'As a man is wont to speak to his friend'
n: The Lord spoke to Moses 'face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend'. No other figure in the Old Testament is given this intimacy — and yet a few verses later Moses cannot see God's face and live. Both are true: friendship, and unbridgeable distance.

Moses, God's friend, asks to see his glory and is allowed only to see him pass from behind. No one sees God and lives — until John writes, 'we saw his glory' (John 1:14). The cleft of the rock where Moses hid became, for the Fathers, the wounded side of Christ.

'The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and of much compassion, and true' — this self-description is quoted more often inside the Old Testament than any other verse (Psalms, Joel, Jonah, Nehemiah). Mercy comes first and reaches 'thousands'; punishment 'to the third and fourth generation' — the household living under one roof.

Cloven hoof and chewing the cud: the origin of kosher law. Explanations range from hygiene to symbolism — creatures that fit their category cleanly are 'clean'. Jesus 'made all meats clean' (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision in Acts 10 opens the table to Gentiles; observant Jews keep the rules to this day.

Two goats: one sacrificed, one sent into the desert carrying the people's sins. Jerome's caper emissarius gave English its word 'scapegoat'. Yom Kippur is still the holiest day of the Jewish year; Hebrews 9 reads the whole ritual as a sketch of Christ entering heaven with his own blood.

t: 'Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy'
n: The refrain of the 'Holiness Code' (Leviticus 17–26). Holiness means set apart, belonging to God — and the chapter that follows applies it to harvest gleanings for the poor, honest weights, wages paid on time, and not cursing the deaf. 1 Peter 1:16 quotes the verse for Christians.

Buried in a chapter of ritual and civil laws is the verse Jesus called the second greatest commandment. Leviticus goes on (19:34) to extend it to the stranger 'as one of the same country'. Rabbi Akiva called this verse 'the great principle of the Torah'.

Every fiftieth year debts are cancelled, slaves freed and land returned to its original families — a built-in reset against permanent poverty. The word comes from yobel, the ram's horn that announced it. Jesus opens his ministry by reading Isaiah 61 — 'to preach the acceptable year of the Lord' — the Jubilee proclaimed for good (Luke 4).

'The Lord bless thee and keep thee; the Lord show his face to thee...' — the oldest biblical text ever found, inscribed on silver amulets from about 600 BC. Its threefold form led Christians to hear the Trinity; it still closes services in synagogues and churches alike.

Twelve spies, forty days, a cluster of grapes so large two men carry it on a pole — and then panic: 'we seemed like locusts'. Only Caleb and Josue trust God. The whole generation is condemned to die in the desert; the forty years of wandering follow from this one night of fear.

Bitten by fiery serpents, the people are healed by looking at a bronze serpent lifted on a pole — the cause of death becomes the sign of healing. Jesus makes it the first explanation of the cross: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up' (John 3:14).

A pagan prophet hired to curse Israel is rebuked by his own donkey, who sees the angel he cannot. The comedy is deliberate: the seer is blind, the beast sees. Balaam ends by blessing Israel instead and uttering the oracle of the star out of Jacob (24:17) — which the Magi were later thought to have followed.

t: 'A star shall rise out of Jacob'
n: Balaam's final oracle: 'a star shall rise out of Jacob and a sceptre shall spring up from Israel'. Jews applied it to David and later to Bar Kochba ('son of the star'), leader of the revolt of AD 132; Christians to the Magi's star. It appears on the coins of the Jewish revolt.

Deuteronomy means 'second law': Moses on the plains of Moab retelling Sinai to the children of those who stood there. The Sabbath commandment here is grounded not in creation, as in Exodus, but in the Exodus — 'remember that thou also didst serve in Egypt'. Rest is a freedom you were denied.

'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' — the creed Jews recite morning and evening and bind on arm and forehead (tefillin) and doorpost (mezuzah). Jesus quotes it as the first and greatest commandment (Mark 12:29). 'Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart' turns law into love.

Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like himself. Israel waited for 'the Prophet' (see John 1:21, 6:14), and Peter in Acts 3:22 says that prophet is Jesus. Deuteronomy ends by noting no such prophet had yet appeared (34:10).

Fourteen verses of blessing, fifty-four of curse: siege, famine, exile, 'thou shalt be scattered among all people'. The exiles of 586 BC read this chapter as their own history foretold, which is why Deuteronomy shaped the books of Kings. The theology — obey and prosper — is what Job argues against.

t: 'The word is very nigh unto thee'
n: The commandment is not in heaven or beyond the sea; it is 'in thy mouth and in thy heart'. Paul lifts this whole passage into Romans 10 and applies it to faith in Christ: the word you need is not far away.

Moses sees the promised land from Mount Nebo and dies without entering it, buried by God himself in a grave 'no man hath known'. Jewish tradition says he died 'by the kiss of God'. Moses' unfinished journey haunts the New Testament: he finally stands in the land at the Transfiguration (Matt 17).

A Canaanite prostitute hides Israel's spies and hangs a scarlet cord from her window. She is saved, joins Israel, and appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Hebrews and James both hold her up as a model — of faith and of works respectively. The scarlet cord was read by the Fathers as the blood of Christ.

No siege engines, only priests, trumpets and a week of silent marching. The conquest is presented as God's act, with Israel's part being obedience. Archaeology finds Jericho's walls fell several times over the centuries; the text is less a war report than a liturgy of trust.

t: 'Choose this day whom you will serve'
n: Joshua's farewell at Sichem puts the choice starkly and answers for himself: 'as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord'. The covenant is renewed by free choice, not inheritance — the pattern every generation must repeat.

A woman judges Israel under a palm tree and leads it to war; another, Jahel, hammers a tent-peg through the fleeing general's skull. Chapter 5, the Song of Debbora, is among the oldest poetry in the Bible. Judges is a spiral of decline — 'every one did that which seemed right to himself' — and its heroes are increasingly flawed.

Gideon asks God for a sign twice — dew on the fleece and not the ground, then the reverse. God patiently obliges. Medieval readers saw the dew-soaked fleece as the Virgin Mary receiving the Word 'as rain upon the fleece' (Ps 71:6 in the Vulgate).

The strongest man in Israel is undone by nagging: 'she pressed him much... his soul fainted away'. Samson's story is the tragedy of gifts without discipline, and yet Hebrews 11 names him among the heroes of faith. His death, killing more in his death than in his life, was read as a shadow of the cross.

A Moabite widow refuses to leave her Israelite mother-in-law: 'whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go... thy God my God'. Ruth, a foreigner, becomes the great-grandmother of David and stands in Jesus' family tree — the book's quiet argument that God's people is entered by loyalty, not birth.

The village women name the child Obed, 'father of Isai, the father of David'. The book's last word is 'David': a story of two widows gleaning barley turns out to be the beginning of the royal line — and, through Matthew 1, of Jesus. Booz the redeemer became a type of Christ.

The boy Samuel hears his name three times in the night and thinks it is the old priest calling. Eli, whose own sons are corrupt, teaches him the answer. 'The word of the Lord was precious in those days' — rare — and it comes to a child.

'Give us a king to judge us, as all nations have.' God takes it personally — 'they have not rejected thee, but me' — yet grants it, after Samuel lists what kings do: conscript your sons, tax your fields, take your daughters. The monarchy begins under a shadow it never entirely escapes.

Saul keeps the best sheep of Amalec 'to sacrifice to the Lord' and is rejected as king for it. Samuel's answer became a prophetic slogan: God wants obedience, not offerings. From here Saul's decline is unstoppable — jealousy, madness, the witch of Endor, death on Gelboe.

t: 'Man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart'
n: Samuel is ready to anoint the tall eldest son; God chooses the youngest, out with the sheep. David's anointing sets the pattern for the Messiah ('anointed one'). The verse became a proverb in every language the Bible touched.

The shepherd refuses Saul's armour and takes five smooth stones. His speech before the fight — 'thou comest to me with a sword... but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts' — is the point of the story. It has served as the emblem of every small cause facing a giant since.

Forbidden by his own law, Saul consults a medium the night before his last battle and the ghost of Samuel rises, furious, to announce his death. Theologians argued whether it was really Samuel or a demon; the text takes it as Samuel. It is the Bible's only séance, told with dread.

t: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
n: 'How are the valiant fallen!' — David mourns the king who hunted him and the friend who loved him 'beyond the love of women'. He orders it taught to Judah as the Song of the Bow. It is grief without a word of triumph; Israel's greatest king begins his reign by weeping for his rival.

David wants to build God a house (a temple); God answers that he will build David a house (a dynasty): 'thy throne shall be firm for ever'. This oracle is the root of all messianic hope — Gabriel quotes it to Mary (Luke 1:32–33). When the dynasty fell in 586 BC, the promise had to be understood on a larger scale.

After David has taken Bethsabee and had her husband killed, the prophet Nathan tells him a story about a rich man who steals a poor man's one lamb. David explodes in anger — and Nathan turns it on him. David's two words of reply, 'I have sinned', are the seed of Psalm 50 (51), the Miserere.

t: 'My son Absalom, would God I might die for thee'
n: Absalom rebelled against his father, and David's men killed him against orders as he hung by his hair from an oak. The king's grief — 'Absalom my son, my son' — is the rawest cry of a parent in the Bible. The fathers saw a father who would die in his son's place; Faulkner took his title from it.

Two women, one living child, and an order to cut it in half. The real mother gives the baby up rather than see him die. The story shows wisdom as insight into the human heart, not cleverness — and it made 'a judgment of Solomon' a phrase in every European language.

'If heaven and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house?' Solomon's prayer knows the paradox of a God who fills everything choosing one place to be found. The Temple (about 960 BC) stood four centuries; its site is the Temple Mount, where the Dome of the Rock now stands.

A foreign widow with a handful of meal and a little oil shares her last meal with the prophet, and neither runs out through the famine. Jesus cites her, with Naaman, to say God's favour has always crossed borders — and Nazareth tries to throw him off a cliff for it (Luke 4:26).

'How long do you halt between two sides?' Elias (Elijah) sets one altar against four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, mocks their god ('perhaps he is asleep'), drenches his own sacrifice in water, and fire falls. It is the great showdown of the Old Testament; Carmelite monks still trace their origin to this mountain.

Fleeing for his life, Elias meets God on Horeb — not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in 'a whistling of a gentle air' (sibilus auræ tenuis). The God of Sinai's thunder now speaks in a whisper. It is one of the Bible's quietest and most quoted moments.

Naboth will not sell his ancestral vineyard; Queen Jezabel arranges false witnesses and a stoning. Elias meets Achab in the vineyard: 'Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?' The prophets' role in Israel — confronting kings over land and blood — is nowhere clearer.

t: Elias taken up in a chariot of fire
n: Because Elias did not die, Israel expected him to return before the Messiah (Mal 4:5); a chair is still left for him at Passover. Jesus says John the Baptist was the Elias who was to come (Matt 11:14). Eliseus' request for a 'double portion' is the share of a firstborn heir.

A Syrian general expects a grand ritual and is told to bathe in a muddy river. His servants' logic — 'if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing...' — persuades him. Jesus cites Naaman as proof that God's grace reaches beyond Israel (Luke 4:27), and the Fathers saw baptism in the seven dips.

t: The book found in the Temple
n: Repairs to the Temple under King Josias (622 BC) turn up 'the book of the law' — probably a form of Deuteronomy — and the young king tears his garments on hearing it read. The reform that followed centralised worship in Jerusalem and shaped how the rest of the Old Testament was edited.

Nabuchodonosor's general burns the Temple, breaks down the walls and deports the people to Babylon. Everything the story had built since Abraham — land, king, temple — is gone in one chapter. Out of this catastrophe come Lamentations, Ezechiel, the second half of Isaiah, and a faith that could survive without a temple.

Chronicles was written after the Exile for a community with no king. It retells Samuel and Kings with the dark episodes (Bethsabee, Absalom) left out, and gives the promise to David an even longer horizon: 'I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom for ever'.

At the dedication of the Temple God promises that repentance can reverse drought, locusts and plague. The verse became a favourite of national prayer movements. In context it belongs to Solomon's Temple and Israel's covenant; the Chronicler wrote it for exiles wondering whether return was still possible.

A pagan Persian king ends the Babylonian exile, and Isaiah 45 had already called him the Lord's 'anointed'. The decree (also known from the Cyrus Cylinder) let subject peoples return and rebuild their temples. Ezra and Nehemiah tell the slow, contested rebuilding of Jerusalem.

Ezra reads the Torah from dawn to noon while Levites 'explained the sense' — the origin of the synagogue habit of reading and homily, and so of the Christian liturgy of the Word. The people weep, then are told to feast: 'the joy of the Lord is our strength'.

Old Tobias's advice to his son: give according to your means, 'turn not away thy face from any poor person', for 'alms deliver from all sin and from death'. This is the Old Testament source of the Jewish and Catholic conviction that charity has power before God; the Golden Rule appears in its negative form at 4:16.

The travelling companion 'Azarias' turns out to be Raphael, 'one of the seven who stand before the Lord'. Tobit's teaching on almsgiving, burial of the dead and prayer made it a favourite of the early Church; Protestant Bibles place it among the Apocrypha. The dog that follows Tobias is one of the Bible's few pets.

Sackcloth, ashes, and a prayer that God is 'the God of the humble, the helper of the little ones... the saviour of them that are without hope'. Judith goes to war armed with beauty and this prayer. Her thanksgiving song (chapter 16) echoes Debbora's, and Mary's Magnificat echoes both.

A widow of Bethulia enters the enemy camp, charms the Assyrian general and cuts off his head with his own sword. Painters from Caravaggio to Artemisia Gentileschi made it their subject. The book is a theological novel — its geography and history are deliberately impossible — about faith that acts.

Mardochai's message to Queen Esther: if she keeps silent, deliverance will come from elsewhere, but perhaps she was made queen for this very moment. The Hebrew Esther never mentions God; the Greek additions (Vulgate chapters 10–16) supply the prayers the Hebrew leaves out.

Found only in the Greek additions (Vulgate chapter 14), Esther strips off her royal robes, covers her head with ashes and prays: 'O my Lord, who alone art our king, help me a desolate woman'. It supplies what the Hebrew Esther left unsaid — that her courage was prayed for first.

'Satan' here is a title — 'the accuser', a prosecuting angel among 'the sons of God' — not yet the devil of later theology. His wager: does Job serve God for nothing? The whole book tests whether love of God can survive when every reward is stripped away.

t: 'The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away'
n: Job's first response to losing everything is worship. 'Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return' is recited at Jewish funerals and quoted at Christian ones. Note that the book does not leave him there — thirty chapters of protest follow.

t: Job curses the day of his birth
n: After seven days of silence with his friends, Job speaks — and the patient Job of chapters 1–2 vanishes. From here to chapter 37 the book is poetry: three cycles of speeches in which the friends defend God's justice and Job demands a hearing. The book honours the protest more than the defence.

t: 'Man born of a woman, living for a short time'
n: 'Cometh forth like a flower, and is destroyed, and fleeth as a shadow.' Job's meditation on mortality; the Book of Common Prayer put it in the burial service. The chapter goes on to ask, 'Shall man that is dead live again?' — and cannot yet answer.

Job's cry of hope in the middle of despair. Jerome's Latin — 'in the last day I shall rise out of the earth, and in my flesh I shall see my God' — reads it as a prophecy of resurrection, and Handel set it in Messiah. The Hebrew is harder and more ambiguous; Job wants a vindicator, and gets one in chapter 42.

A poem on mining — men dig for silver, sapphires, gold in the dark — that turns to ask where wisdom is mined. Not in the sea, not for gold; 'God understandeth the way of it'. The answer given to man is only: 'the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom'. The Bible's most beautiful poem about the limits of knowledge.

t: God answers out of the whirlwind
n: God does not explain Job's suffering. Instead he asks seventy questions about creation: 'Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?' The answer to the problem of evil offered here is not an argument but an encounter — and Job says it is enough (42:5).

t: God sides with Job against the friends
n: The twist: God says the friends, who defended him, 'have not spoken the thing that is right before me, as my servant Job hath'. Honest anger at God is closer to him than tidy theology. Job must pray for his comforters, and his fortunes are restored double.

Psalm 1 was placed first as the entrance to the whole Psalter: two ways, the just and the wicked, and a tree planted by running waters. 'Meditate' (meditabitur) meant murmuring the text aloud — how the psalms were always meant to be used.

t: 'Thou art my son, this day have I begotten thee'
n: A coronation psalm for the kings of Judah becomes the New Testament's favourite text about Jesus: quoted at his baptism and transfiguration, in Acts 13 and three times in Hebrews. Vulgate numbering: this is Psalm 2 in all traditions.

t: 'What is man, that thou art mindful of him?'
n: Awe at the night sky turns to awe at human dignity: 'a little less than the angels' (the Hebrew says 'than God'). Hebrews 2 applies it to Christ, crowned after being made lower. Neil Armstrong's crewmate Buzz Aldrin read this psalm on the moon.

t: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'
n: Vulgate Psalm 21 is Psalm 22 in Hebrew and most English Bibles. Jesus quoted its first line from the cross; the psalm goes on to describe pierced hands and feet, mocking, and lots cast for clothing, then turns into praise. Read all of it to hear what Jesus was praying.

t: 'The Lord ruleth me' — the shepherd psalm
n: Vulgate Psalm 22 is the beloved Psalm 23 of the Hebrew numbering. Jerome's Dominus regit me ('the Lord rules me') is the Douay's odd 'ruleth'; the Hebrew is 'the Lord is my shepherd'. Green pastures, still waters, the valley of the shadow of death, a table and an overflowing cup.

t: 'As the hart panteth after the fountains of water'
n: Psalm 41 (Hebrew 42) opens the second book of the Psalter with an exile's homesickness for the Temple: 'my soul hath thirsted after the strong living God'. It was sung as the newly baptised approached the font at Easter, and deer drinking at streams decorate early Christian baptisteries.

Psalm 50 (51 in Hebrew numbering): David's repentance after Nathan's rebuke. 'Create a clean heart in me, O God' and 'a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise'. Allegri's setting was so prized that the Vatican forbade copies — until the fourteen-year-old Mozart wrote it out from memory.

Psalm 83 (Hebrew 84): a pilgrim's psalm, in love with the Temple courts, envying the sparrow that nests near the altar. 'Better is one day in thy courts above thousands.' Brahms set it in the German Requiem.

t: 'He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High'
n: Psalm 90 (Hebrew 91): the psalm of protection, prayed at Compline every night. Satan quotes verses 11–12 to Jesus in the desert ('he hath given his angels charge over thee') — proof that the devil can quote Scripture.

Psalm 94 (Hebrew 95) opens the Church's daily prayer every morning: 'Come let us praise the Lord with joy'. Its second half turns to warning — 'today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts' — which Hebrews 3–4 develops into a whole sermon on 'today'.

t: 'As a father hath compassion on his children'
n: Psalm 102 (Hebrew 103): 'as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us... he knoweth our frame, he remembereth that we are dust'. The psalm quotes Exodus 34's 'merciful and gracious' and turns it into song.

Psalm 109 (Hebrew 110) is the psalm the New Testament quotes most. 'Sit thou at my right hand' — Jesus asks how David can call his own descendant 'Lord' (Matt 22:44). 'Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech' is the foundation of Hebrews' theology of Christ's priesthood.

Psalm 117 (Hebrew 118) was sung at Passover and on Palm Sunday: 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord'. Jesus applies the rejected stone to himself (Matt 21:42), and Peter to the resurrection (Acts 4:11). 'This is the day which the Lord hath made' is the Church's Easter refrain.

t: 'Thy word is a lamp to my feet'
n: Psalm 118 (Hebrew 119) is the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses in twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, every verse but one naming the Law. Monks divided it across the daytime hours; it is a love poem to God's word.

Psalm 129 (Hebrew 130): 'Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord'. The great psalm of penance and hope, prayed for the dead in the Catholic tradition and the source of Oscar Wilde's title. 'With the Lord there is mercy, and with him plentiful redemption.'

Psalm 136 (Hebrew 137): the exiles hang up their harps and refuse to sing for their captors. The psalm's last verse, blessing the one who dashes Babylon's infants against the rock, is one of the Bible's most disturbing lines — raw grief that the Church omits from public prayer but keeps in the book.

t: 'Lord, thou hast proved me, and known me'
n: Psalm 138 (Hebrew 139): the psalm of God's inescapable presence — 'if I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present' — and of God knitting the psalmist in the womb. Its meditation on being known has made it a favourite of contemplatives and of those praying for the unborn.

The Psalter ends in pure praise: trumpets, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, organs and cymbals. 'Let every spirit praise the Lord' — thirteen 'praise' in six verses. The five books of Psalms move from the lament of the individual to the praise of everything that breathes.

t: 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom'
n: Not terror but reverence — living as if God is real. This motto governs Proverbs, and Job 28, Psalm 110 and Sirach 1 repeat it. Proverbs collects sayings attributed to Solomon and others; its wisdom is practical, earthy and international, shared with Egypt and Mesopotamia.

'Have confidence in the Lord with all thy heart... in all thy ways think on him, and he will direct thy steps.' Among the most memorised verses in the Bible. Proverbs 1–9 is a father's instruction to a son, framing the short sayings that follow.

Wisdom speaks as a person: 'The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways... I was with him forming all things'. Fourth-century Christians fought over whether the Vulgate's 'possessed' or the Greek 'created' applied to Christ; John's 'In the beginning was the Word' grows from this soil.

An acrostic poem — each verse starts with the next Hebrew letter — praising a woman who runs an estate, trades, gives to the poor, and 'shall laugh in the latter day'. Jewish husbands sing it to their wives on Friday nights. 'Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: the woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.'

Hebrew hevel — breath, vapour, mist. Ecclesiastes (Qoheleth, 'the Preacher') is the Bible's sceptic: work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth all pass; 'there is nothing new under the sun'. The rabbis nearly excluded it; it stayed because it ends with 'fear God and keep his commandments' and because it is true.

'A time to be born and a time to die... a time to weep and a time to laugh' — fourteen pairs. The passage became a folk song in the 1960s. Its point is not resignation but that no season is permanent, and that God 'hath made all things good in their time'.

t: Old age as a house falling in
n: 'Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth' opens the Bible's most beautiful description of aging: the keepers of the house tremble (arms), the grinders are few (teeth), the windows darken (eyes), the almond tree flowers (white hair), 'and the dust return into its earth... and the spirit return to God'.

A collection of love poems, frankly erotic, with no mention of God. Israel read it as the love between the Lord and his people; the Church as Christ and the Church, or Christ and the soul. Rabbi Akiva called it 'the holy of holies' of Scripture; Bernard of Clairvaux preached eighty-six sermons and only reached chapter 2.

'For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in our land.' The Song's most quoted lyric — spring as the season of love. Monastic writers heard Christ calling the soul; the Church reads it on the feast of the Visitation.

The climax of the Song: love is a seal on the heart, 'its lamps are fire and flames', and 'many waters cannot quench' it. This is the closest the Old Testament comes to saying that love outlasts death — quoted at weddings and funerals alike.

t: The wicked plot against the just man
n: 'Let us examine him by outrages and tortures... let us condemn him to a most shameful death.' Written in Greek in Alexandria a century before Christ, this passage reads like a script of Good Friday; the Church reads it in Holy Week. Wisdom is deuterocanonical, absent from Jewish and Protestant Bibles.

t: 'The souls of the just are in the hand of God'
n: 'They seemed, in the eyes of the unwise, to die... but they are in peace.' The first clear Old Testament statement of immortality, written under Greek influence. It is the most common reading at Catholic funerals.

Twenty-one attributes of Wisdom (three times seven): 'a vapour of the power of God... the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty'. Hebrews 1:3 describes the Son in these terms. Together with Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24 this is the Old Testament root of the doctrine of the Word.

Written in Hebrew by Jesus ben Sirach in Jerusalem about 180 BC and translated into Greek by his grandson, this is the longest wisdom book. Its Latin name Ecclesiasticus, 'the church book', comes from how much the early Church used it for teaching converts. Hebrew fragments were found at Qumran and Masada.

Sirach expands the fourth commandment into a whole chapter: care for a father in old age, 'and if his understanding fail, have patience with him'. It is read on the feast of the Holy Family. Sirach is the most 'practical' book of the Bible, on everything from table manners to lending money.

t: Wisdom pitches her tent in Israel
n: Wisdom, who 'came out of the mouth of the most High' and circled heaven and earth, is told by the Creator: 'Let thy dwelling be in Jacob'. She becomes the Law of Moses (24:32). John 1:14, 'the Word was made flesh and dwelt (pitched his tent) among us', echoes this chapter. The Church applies it to the Virgin Mary.

t: 'Let us now praise men of renown'
n: A roll-call of Israel's heroes from Enoch to Nehemiah — Sirach's history of the world in portraits. James Agee borrowed the opening for his book on Alabama tenant farmers, turning the praise toward the unknown: 'and some there be which have no memorial'.

t: 'They shall turn their swords into ploughshares'
n: All nations stream to the mountain of the Lord's house; war is unlearned. The words are carved outside the United Nations. Micheas 4 has the same oracle almost word for word; Joel 3 reverses it ('beat your ploughshares into swords') — the Bible arguing with itself about the last days.

In the Temple, the year King Ozias died (about 740 BC), Isaias sees the Lord enthroned and the seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy' — the Sanctus sung at every Mass. His lips are cleansed with a coal, and he volunteers: 'Lo, here am I, send me'.

The most disputed verse between Jews and Christians. Hebrew almah means 'young woman'; the Greek Septuagint chose parthenos, 'virgin', and Matthew 1:23 quotes that. In context the sign concerns a child born in King Achaz's own day; Christians read a second, fuller meaning. Compare the JPS reading in this app.

'Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace' — the names of a royal child, sung at Christmas since Handel. Originally an accession oracle for a king of Judah, perhaps Ezechias; the Church reads it at Midnight Mass.

t: The rod out of the root of Jesse
n: A shoot from a felled stump: the Davidic dynasty cut down but sprouting again. The seven gifts of the Spirit in Catholic teaching come from verses 2–3 (the Vulgate's 'piety' making the Hebrew six into seven). The wolf dwelling with the lamb is the Bible's picture of creation restored.

t: The feast on the mountain, death destroyed
n: 'A feast of fat things, a feast of wine... he shall cast death down headlong for ever, and the Lord God shall wipe away tears from every face.' Revelation 21:4 quotes this; it is read at funerals and gives the Mass its image of the heavenly banquet.

Chapter 40 opens the 'Book of Consolation' (Isaias 40–55), addressed to the exiles in Babylon a century and a half after the prophet of chapter 1 — most scholars speak of a 'Second Isaias'. 'The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare ye the way of the Lord' is applied by all four Gospels to John the Baptist.

The fourth 'Servant Song' begins here and runs through chapter 53. Who is the servant — Israel, the prophet, a future figure? Jews have mostly read Israel; Christians since Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8) have read Jesus. Read the JPS alongside the Vulgate to see how the ambiguity plays.

'Despised and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows... he was wounded for our iniquities... as a sheep before her shearers, he shall be dumb.' No Old Testament chapter is quoted more in the New Testament passion narratives. The servant suffers not for his own sins but for others' — the heart of the Christian reading of the cross.

t: 'All you that thirst, come to the waters'
n: Free wine and milk, 'without money and without any price'; God's thoughts higher than ours 'as the heavens are exalted above the earth'; and the word that 'shall not return to me void' but does what it was sent for. The chapter closes the Book of Consolation and is read at the Easter Vigil.

Not bowing the head like a bulrush, but loosing the bands of wickedness, feeding the hungry, housing the homeless — 'then shall thy light break forth as the morning'. The Church reads this on the Friday after Ash Wednesday, to say at the start of Lent what fasting is for.

t: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me'
n: The passage Jesus unrolled in the synagogue of Nazareth and then said, 'This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears' (Luke 4:21). Good news to the poor, liberty to captives, the year of the Lord's favour — a jubilee proclamation.

'Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee.' Jeremias protests that he is a child; God touches his mouth. His forty-year ministry (627–586 BC) ends in the ruin he foretold, and he weeps through it — 'the weeping prophet'. He is the Old Testament figure most like Jesus in his suffering.

Jeremias' most intimate complaint: God has seduced (the Hebrew is that strong) and overpowered him; he is a daily laughing-stock; yet when he tries to stop, the word is 'a burning fire shut up in my bones'. No prophet argues with God more bitterly or stays more faithful.

Build houses, plant gardens, marry, 'seek the peace of the city to which I have caused you to be carried away' — and after seventy years I will bring you back. Jeremias tells the exiles to settle in Babylon instead of waiting for quick rescue; verse 11, 'thoughts of peace and not of affliction', is one of the most quoted in Scripture.

The only place the Old Testament uses the phrase: a covenant written 'in their heart', where 'all shall know me, from the least of them even to the greatest'. Hebrews 8 quotes the whole passage; Jesus' words 'the new testament in my blood' at the Last Supper point here.

t: 'The mercies of the Lord... are new every morning'
n: Lamentations is five poems over the burnt city of 586 BC, four of them alphabetical acrostics — grief given a form. At the exact centre of the book comes this turn to hope: 'his mercies are new every morning; great is thy faithfulness'. The Church sings Lamentations in the dark of Holy Week (Tenebrae).

Baruch, Jeremias' secretary, is placed after Lamentations in Catholic Bibles. Its poem on wisdom ends, in the Vulgate, 'afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men' (3:38) — read by the Fathers as a prophecy of the Incarnation. Chapter 6, the 'Letter of Jeremias', mocks idols.

Four living creatures with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle), wheels within wheels full of eyes, and a throne above — God appears to the exiles beside a Babylonian canal, showing he is not confined to Jerusalem's Temple. The four faces became the symbols of the four evangelists; Jewish mysticism (merkavah) grew from this chapter.

After denouncing Israel's leaders as shepherds who feed themselves, God announces that he will shepherd the flock personally — seeking the lost, binding the broken. Jesus' 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10) and the parable of the lost sheep are this chapter made flesh.

t: 'A new heart... a heart of flesh'
n: 'I will pour upon you clean water... and I will give you a new heart, and put a new spirit within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh.' Water, heart, spirit — the vocabulary of baptism. Read at the Easter Vigil beside the font.

'Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?' The bones knit, the flesh comes, and the breath (ruach — also 'wind' and 'spirit') enters them. Written for exiles who said 'our hope is lost', it is the Old Testament's clearest picture of national resurrection and, for Christians, of the resurrection of the body.

Gold, silver, brass, iron mixed with clay — four empires, then a stone 'cut out of a mountain without hands' that shatters them and fills the earth. Daniel's scheme of successive kingdoms shaped Jewish and Christian views of history for two thousand years; the stone was read as Christ's kingdom.

t: The song of the three young men
n: In the Vulgate, the three youths in the furnace sing a long canticle (verses 24–90) that the Hebrew Daniel lacks: 'All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord' — the Benedicite, sung on Sundays and feasts in the Divine Office. The mysterious fourth figure in the fire, 'like the son of God', was read as Christ or an angel.

Baltassar drinks from the Temple vessels at a feast; fingers write on the plaster. Daniel reads: Mane, Thecel, Phares — numbered, weighed, divided. 'Thou art weighed in the balance, and art found wanting.' That night Babylon falls (539 BC). The English idiom 'the writing on the wall' comes from here.

Trapped by a law his rivals engineered, Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem three times a day and is thrown to the lions; the king cannot sleep, and finds him unharmed at dawn. The story was among the earliest painted in the catacombs — a Christian facing the arena saw himself in it.

Coming 'with the clouds of heaven' to the Ancient of Days and receiving an everlasting kingdom. This is the source of Jesus' favourite title for himself, and of his answer to the high priest, 'you shall see the Son of man... coming in the clouds' (Mark 14:62), which sealed his condemnation.

Seventy 'weeks' of years until 'the Holy of holies may be anointed' and 'Christ shall be slain' (Vulgate). This dense prophecy has been calculated in every century — from the Maccabean crisis to the crucifixion to the end of the world. Its original horizon is the desecration of the Temple in 167 BC.

A young woman falsely accused of adultery by two elders who tried to seduce her; young Daniel cross-examines them separately and exposes the lie. Preserved only in Greek, it is chapter 13 in the Vulgate and 'apocryphal' in Protestant Bibles. Rembrandt and many others painted the bathing scene.

Jesus quotes this verse twice in Matthew (9:13, 12:7), each time to Pharisees: 'go and learn what this meaneth'. Hebrew hesed — loyal love, covenant kindness — is what God wants more than ritual. Osee's whole book is about love that keeps going after betrayal.

t: 'I called my son out of Egypt'
n: God as a father teaching a toddler to walk, lifting him to his cheek. Matthew 2:15 applies 'out of Egypt have I called my son' to the Holy Family's return. Osee's own marriage to an unfaithful wife (chapters 1–3) is the book's living parable of God's stubborn love for Israel.

t: 'I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh'
n: 'Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy... your young men shall see visions.' Peter's Pentecost sermon opens with this passage (Acts 2:17): the Spirit for everyone, not only prophets and kings. Vulgate numbering places these verses in chapter 2 (Hebrew Bibles begin chapter 3 here).

God rejects feasts, sacrifices and hymns from a people who cheat the poor: 'take away from me the tumult of thy songs'. Amos, a shepherd from Tecua sent to the prosperous northern kingdom, is the prophet of social justice; Martin Luther King quoted this verse in 'I have a dream'.

t: A famine of hearing the word
n: 'Not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord.' Amos threatens the worst punishment: silence from God. His book ends (9:11–15) with the fallen tent of David rebuilt — a passage James quotes at the Council of Jerusalem to admit the Gentiles (Acts 15:16).

t: Jonas in the belly of the fish
n: Three days in the fish, and a psalm prayed from inside it. Jesus calls it the only sign he will give — 'as Jonas was in the whale's belly three days... so shall the Son of man be in the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40). The book is a satire on a prophet who resents God's mercy toward Nineveh.

Out of the smallest clan of Judah 'shall come forth unto me he that is to be the ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity'. When Herod asks where the Christ is to be born, the scribes quote this verse (Matt 2:6).

t: 'What doth the Lord require of thee?'
n: 'To do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God.' The prophets' summary of religion in one line, preferred to 'thousands of rams'. It appears on countless walls and became the motto of humanitarian movements.

A century after Jonas, Nineveh has not stayed repentant. Nahum exults over its destruction (612 BC) — 'behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings', a line Isaias 52 and Romans 10 also use. The Bible keeps both books: mercy for Nineveh and judgment on it.

t: 'The just shall live in his faith'
n: Habacuc complains that God tolerates evil; God answers that the vision will come and 'the just shall live in his faith'. Paul builds Romans and Galatians on this half-verse; Luther's reading of it began the Reformation. Hebrew emunah is closer to 'faithfulness' than to belief.

t: 'Although the fig tree shall not blossom'
n: Habacuc's closing prayer: crops fail, flocks vanish, 'but I will rejoice in the Lord'. Faith with nothing left to lean on. The verse has comforted farmers and the bereaved alike; the chapter is a psalm, complete with musical directions.

t: 'The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty'
n: After two chapters of the 'day of the Lord' — Sophonias gave the Church the Dies iræ — the book turns to joy: 'he will rejoice over thee with gladness... he will be silent in his love'. Read on the third Sunday of Advent (Gaudete) and, by Luke's echo, behind Gabriel's greeting to Mary.

t: 'The desired of all nations shall come'
n: Aggeus urges the returned exiles (520 BC) to rebuild the Temple; to those who remember Solomon's, the new one looks like nothing. God promises: 'the glory of this last house shall be greater than the first'. Jerome's 'the desired of all nations' became a title of Christ and an Advent hymn.

t: The king riding on a donkey
n: 'Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Sion... thy king will come to thee, the just and saviour: he is poor, and riding upon an ass.' Jesus stages his entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday to fulfil this verse (Matt 21:5). A king on a donkey, not a war-horse: peace, not conquest.

t: 'They shall look upon me, whom they have pierced'
n: A mysterious oracle of mourning over one pierced, 'as one mourneth for an only son'. John 19:37 quotes it as the soldier's spear enters Jesus' side, and Revelation 1:7 makes it the watchword of the Second Coming. Zacharias 9–14 is quoted in the passion narratives more than any other prophet except Isaias.

'From the rising of the sun even to the going down, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation.' From the second century the Church read this as a prophecy of the Eucharist offered worldwide; it is quoted in the Roman Canon's tradition.

'Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face' — 'Malachias' means 'my messenger', so the prophet's name is his message. Jesus applies the verse to John the Baptist (Matt 11:10); 'the Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple' is read on Candlemas, when the infant is carried in.

t: 'I will send you Elias the prophet'
n: The last words of the Old Testament in the Christian ordering: Elias will return before 'the great and dreadful day' to turn hearts of fathers to children. Luke 1:17 applies this to John the Baptist. Vulgate numbering: some Bibles place these verses at the end of chapter 3.

When a royal officer demands pagan sacrifice at Modin, the priest Mathathias kills him and the collaborator and flees to the hills with his sons — Judas Maccabeus among them. Written in Hebrew about 100 BC, 1 Maccabees is our main source for the revolt commemorated at Hanukkah (4:36–59).

t: The mother and her seven sons
n: Seven brothers tortured to death one after another for refusing pork, encouraged by their mother, each confessing hope in bodily resurrection: 'the King of the world will raise us up'. The clearest Old Testament statement of resurrection, and the model for the Christian martyr narratives.

t: 'It is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead'
n: Judas sends money to Jerusalem for a sacrifice on behalf of fallen soldiers found with pagan amulets. Catholic teaching on purgatory and prayer for the dead cites this verse; its absence from the Hebrew canon was one reason the Reformers set the book aside.
